title: Chicken Do Pyaza
subtitle: A rich Anglo-Indian curry with two stages of onion
excerpt: Do pyaza means double onion. Half the onions cook down into the sauce, the other half go in near the end to stay chunky. The result is a deep, sweet curry with real body.
sourceNotes: Anglo-Indian restaurant tradition, adapted from multiple curry-house and home-cook sources.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze in portions for up to three months. Defrost overnight and reheat gently with a splash of water.
recipe.batchNotes: Double or triple the batch easily. Cook in a wide, heavy pan so the onions brown rather than steam.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Tastes better the next day. Cool fully, refrigerate, and reheat slowly before serving.

content.text: Do pyaza is a north Indian curry built on onions cooked two ways. The first batch melts into the sauce; the second goes in late to keep some texture. Watch the heat when you fry the spices as they catch quickly.
Heat the oil in a wide pan over medium-high heat. Add half the sliced onions with a pinch of salt. Fry for 12 minutes, stirring often, until deep golden brown. Remove and set aside.
Add the garlic and ginger to the pan. Stir for one minute until fragrant. Do not let them burn.
Add the cumin, coriander, turmeric, and chilli powder. Stir for 30 seconds. Add the tinned tomatoes and cook for 8 minutes, stirring, until the oil begins to separate at the edges.
Add the chicken pieces. Stir to coat in the sauce. Season with salt. Add 100ml of water, cover, and cook on a low-medium heat for 20 minutes.
Remove the lid. Add the remaining raw onion slices. Stir and cook uncovered for 8 minutes. The onion should soften slightly but keep some bite.
Stir in the reserved fried onions and the garam masala. Cook for two minutes. Taste and adjust the salt.
Scatter over the fresh coriander and serve with rice or flatbreads.

items.symptom: The sauce is watery and thin.
items.cause: The tomatoes were not cooked down enough before the chicken went in.
items.fix: Simmer uncovered for a few more minutes to reduce. The oil separating from the paste is the signal to add the chicken.

items.symptom: The chicken is dry and stringy.
items.cause: It cooked too fast over too high a heat.
items.fix: Keep the heat low once the chicken is added. A gentle simmer is enough to cook it through without toughening it.

items.cause: The spices were added to a cold pan or not fried long enough.
items.fix: Make sure the oil is hot before adding the spices, and fry them for at least 30 seconds. A pinch more garam masala stirred in at the end also lifts the flavour.
